newsitem.title: USA: Arguments in Army rape trial delayed until Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Arguments in Army rape trial delayed until Thursday.

text.p: The judge in the Army rape trial of Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson said jury instructions and closing arguments in the case will begin Thursday, after wrangling over the instructions took longer than expected.

The six-member jury had earlier been expected to get the case late Wednesday. But Army Trial Judge Col. Paul Johnston said he wanted time to study a prosecution request to let the jury weigh evidence of offences with which Simpson has not been charged in considering his guilt on the charges he faces.
Prosecutor David Thomas said such evidence would demonstrate Simpson had a "common scheme, plan and design," to rape trainees. Johnston was expected to rule on the issue later Wednesday.
The six-member jury will be asked to rule on 19 charges of rape, involving six women, and 35 other counts against Simpson.

Simpson, 32, is the first of 12 trainers charged in a sexual misconduct scandal at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground to go to trial, although four other cases have been resolved through administrative means or plea agreements. He also faces the most rape charges.
He has pleaded innocent to rape and the other charges, but earlier pleaded guilty to 11 counts of improper sexual intercourse with trainees and five counts of propositioning.

Testimony in the case ended Tuesday, after eight days in which prosecutors sought to show Simpson abused his authority to force female trainees at the proving ground's Ordnance Centre and School into having sex with him.
His lawyers argued that Simpson engaged only in consensual sex with the women.
Wednesday's court session was devoted to hammering out fine points of the instructions given to the jury and the findings they will be permitted to reach.

Johnston denied a defence request to tell the jury the credibility of Simpson' alleged victims could be evaluated in light of army rules against sex with drill instructors, which would make them Simpson's accomplices if the sex were consensual.

"They are shifting the blame, and trying to make it look non-consensual," civilian defence attorney Frank Spinner said. "Their motive to lie or misrepresent is to get themselves out of trouble and get him in trouble.

Johnston also said he would allow jurors to consider, in instances where Simpson has been charged with rape, verdicts on lesser charges of indecent assault. He rejected a prosecution request to allow jurors also to consider verdicts of committing an indecent act.

An Army legal liaison told reporters after the session that it appeared Johnston would not in his instructions broaden the military rape law by removing a requirement that fear of death or bodily harm must be present to justify a lack of resistance by the woman involved.

Johnston last week said a drill sergeant's power over trainees created a "unique situation of dominance and control," and rejected a defence request to dismiss rape charges involving four women who had not explicitly resisted sex with Simpson. This sparked speculation he would create a broader definition of rape.

Simpson faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted of rape. He faces a total maximum sentence of 32 years, dishonourable discharge and forfeiture of pay and allowances for the counts to which he has pleaded guilty.

Although the National Organisation for the Advancement of Coloured People and other civil rights supporters have said the investigation that led to charges against Simpson, who is African-American, and the other trainers unfairly targeted blacks in the military, race has not been presented as an issue in the trial.
